title: Freedom of conscience
hookLine: a thread the Gurus did not wear, and the ninth Guru gave his life for others' right to wear it

lines: A COTTON THREAD ACROSS THE CHEST.
THE NINTH GURU DIES FOR IT.
cards: A cotton thread, worn across the chest. For some Hindu families it's the janeu, the sacred thread, put on in a ceremony and worn for life.
In a passage of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak declines that thread and asks instead for one spun from compassion and contentment, a thread that never breaks or burns.
And yet the ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, is remembered for giving his life so that other people could keep wearing theirs. How do the two fit?

teach.b: You've met both halves before: the boy Nanak and the thread, and the pandits arriving at Anandpur. Here's the story as Sikh tradition tells it.
A group of Kashmiri Pandits, Hindu scholars, came to Guru Tegh Bahadur at Anandpur. The Mughal authorities were pressing them to give up their faith and convert.

Tradition says the Guru's young son, the future tenth Guru, was there, and said such a moment needed someone great to stand up. The Guru told the Pandits to send word to the emperor: if he converts, we will too.
Then he went to Delhi. He was arrested and, refusing to give up his faith, he was executed in the city, at a spot Sikhs now mark with Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib.

teach.h: HE GAVE HIS HEAD, NOT HIS RESOLVE.
teach.b: Later, a work attributed to the tenth Guru, the Bachittar Natak, sums it up, paraphrased: he protected their forehead mark and their sacred thread; he gave his head, but not his resolve.
Hold that next to Guru Nanak's hymn. Guru Nanak had set the thread aside; his path had its own way.
And the ninth Guru died for the right of people to keep a way that wasn't his.
That's freedom of conscience, made concrete: not my faith, my right, but their faith, their right. The pressure came from the power of a state, not from the faith of ordinary neighbors.
In Sikh memory, this is a stand against force, not against any people or religion. The Guru's answer wasn't to force anyone back. It was to stand between the weak and the strong, and not move.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom with kirtan, readings of his hymns and gatherings at gurdwaras, including Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Delhi, and speak of him as a defender of the freedom of faith.

o: the freedom to convert others to the faith you hold
a rule that no one should practice any faith in public
everyone's right to keep their own faith, even one not yours

games.q: the story's places and pieces: tap the pairs.
p: where the ninth Guru was executed
he gave his head, not his resolve

s: in Asa di Var, Guru Nanak accepts the sacred thread
he declines it, asking for a thread of compassion and contentment.
tradition says the ninth Guru went to Delhi for the Pandits' freedom
he went to stand for their right to keep their faith.
Sikhs remember this as a stand against a whole religion
it's remembered as a stand against force, not against any people or faith.

games.q: people of another faith come to you. the state is forcing them to convert. their thread is one your own tradition doesn't wear. what do you do?
o: tell them it's not your fight.
suggest they join your path instead.
stand for their right to keep their own faith, at any cost.
games.why: tradition says Guru Tegh Bahadur went to Delhi for them and gave his life there: their faith, their right.

practice: Think of someone whose way of believing, praying or living differs from yours, a coworker who fasts, a neighbor who wears something you don't, a relative who left a tradition or joined one, and hold them in mind with respect.
Then notice where their freedom might be squeezed by a joke or a schedule that ignores their holy day, and find one small way to make room. If you pray, remember Waheguru on each breath.

wordCard.voice: Freedom of conscience. The ninth Guru gave his life for the right of others to keep a faith that wasn't his own. Today's word.

orig.note: faith, duty, the right way; the ninth Guru stood for others' freedom to keep their own.

carryVoice: Your line: their faith, their right. He gave his head, but not his resolve. Rest well.
